title: Terzan 12
caption: Globular cluster Terzan 12, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Terzan 12 · constellation Sagittarius · about 15,000 light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA, ESA/Hubble, Roger Cohen (Rutgers University)

recognition.text: NASA Hubble image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: Hundreds of thousands of stars crowd together in the compact, beehive-like globular cluster Terzan 12. Stars on the left look redder, while those toward the right are bluish-white. The cluster lies about 15,000 light-years away, in the direction of Sagittarius, deep inside the Milky Way.

That color shift does not come from the cluster. Gas and dust between us and Terzan 12 absorb and alter its starlight, scattering blue light away and letting mostly redder wavelengths reach Earth. The dust clouds are patchy, so some parts of the cluster look redder than others along our line of sight.

Not every bright star belongs to the cluster either. The brightest red stars are bloated, aging giants many times larger than the Sun, lying between Earth and Terzan 12, and only a few may be members. The very brightest hot, blue stars also lie along the line of sight rather than inside Terzan 12, which contains only aging stars.

understand.summary: A composite from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3 in visible and infrared light. F606W is shown in blue, F110W in green and F160W in red.
understand.eye: Two of the three filters record infrared light, which the eye cannot see and which passes through dust more easily than visible light.

explore: Our galaxy's outskirts host about 150 ancient globular clusters, which orbit the galactic center far above and below the flat plane of the galaxy. Terzan 12 is one of 11 that the Turkish-Armenian astronomer Agop Terzan discovered approximately a half-century ago. Hubble observations have helped show how age relates to composition in the galaxy's innermost globulars.
